column1: # Hmong class nouns and their members, from Bisang (1993) Appendix II (pp. 42-45)
# A class noun is an ordinary noun that heads a compound and fixes its semantic
# class: ntoo 'tree' heads ntoo ciab 'larch'. Bisang keeps class nouns strictly
# apart from classifiers -- a class noun is referential and part of the noun
# phrase, a classifier is not -- while showing that several forms do both jobs
# (zaj, phau, lo, pob, qhov; pp. 20-24). Those forms therefore appear both here
# CLASS_NOUN is the heading noun, empty where the source lists a member with no
#   class noun (the four birds on p. 43, the agent nouns formed with tus).
# MEMBER is the compound, written as the source writes it, with spaces; the
#   converter joins them with underscores to match the ontology's own convention
#   for multi-word forms (cf. the existing yas_taw 'ankle', headword yas).
# GLOSS is the English gloss the source gives, lightly normalised to a bare noun
#   phrase: "yellow thrush, oriole" is recorded as "yellow thrush", and "slave,
#   servant" as "servant", so that the gloss can be looked up as a lemma.
# CLASSIFIER is the numeral classifier the source says the compound takes, where
# CATEGORY is the ontology category the member belongs in, using the terms
#   already in hmong_ontology.xml's category_set; empty where no existing term
#   fits and one should not be invented.
# DIALECT is WH throughout: Bisang describes White Hmong (p. 45 n. 1).
# SOURCE: B:<page> = Bisang, Walter. 1993. Classifiers, quantifiers and class
#   nouns in Hmong. Studies in Language 17(1): 1-51.
# Rows whose MEMBER is empty record the class noun itself rather than one of its
# members: its own gloss and its own CATEGORY, which the converter needs if the
# form is not already a lemma in the ontology. Thirteen class nouns have only such
# a row, because Bisang names them without listing their members.
